description: We are a team of aspiring developers and innovators participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are interested in space science, satellite imagery, Earth observation, and developing technology-driven solutions to real-world problems. Our skills include programming, research, data visualization, and application development.
summary:
Tanaw is a free web app for farmers in Valencia City, Bukidnon, Philippines. A farmer draws their field on a map and types nothing else. Tanaw reads a year of satellite images to work out which crop the field holds: rice, sugarcane or corn. NASA Earth observations and Sentinel-2 imagery then show its soil and drainage, its planting history since 2020, and the climate it faces.

At the heart of the app is a crop rotation planner built for the Field Shift challenge. It builds about 160 twelve-month rotations from 24 Philippine crops and checks each one against agronomic rules. It then compares them on irrigation water, soil health, nitrogen, climate risk, methane, income and labor. The farmer taps what matters most and the options re-rank instantly.

Tanaw also gives dated next steps and a harvest forecast for each field, damage spotting, and a city-wide view for the City Agriculture Office. A farm assistant explains the results in Cebuano, Filipino or English.

This matters because Valencia's dry-season rain has fallen 12% and nights are warming. Farmers need choices made for their own field, not one calendar for the whole province.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

1. Field check. The farmer draws the field on a map. Each 20 m pixel is classed from its own Sentinel-2 history: rice, sugarcane, corn or upland crop, banana or perennial, idle, or built-up. Tanaw shows how sure it is, and the farmer can correct it with one tap. It then reads drainage, standing water, bare-soil days, crops per year and Bureau of Soils and Water Management (BSWM) soil classes.

2. Rotation planner (the Field Shift core). Tanaw builds about 160 twelve-month rotations from 24 Philippine crops in 10 plant families. Each one is checked against rotation rules: no same plant family in a row, no shared pests in a row, a legume before a crop that needs a lot of nitrogen, and alternating root depth. Each rotation is costed for irrigation water (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration, under 1998-2011 and 2012-2025 rain normals and a 1-in-4 dry year), climate risk (dry spells, waterlogging, heat at flowering), soil health, nitrogen added, methane, income and labor. The farmer taps their priorities (save water, build soil, lower risk, more income, less labor) and the options re-rank instantly.

3. Field report. Planting dates, a health score, dated next steps, a growth-stage replay every 10 days for the past year, damage and stress spotting, a harvest and income forecast, and a comparison with the barangay. The full week-by-week season calendar is built for rice today. Corn and sugarcane get the field check, the soil read and the rotation plan.

4. City view. The same engine runs on every field in Valencia: crop stage, hectares due for harvest, barangay health, and the water, urea and methane the city could save with better rotations.

5. Tanaw Assistant. A chat helper that explains the report in Cebuano, Filipino or English.

6. Take-home report. A printable page or PDF, plus a CSV for the City Agriculture Office.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline on GitHub Actions turns NASA and Sentinel-2 data into small static files: a 10-day history for every farmland pixel, climate normals, and the crop and soil databases. A JavaScript engine runs the whole analysis in the browser in under a second, with no account needed. The same engine code is tested offline against synthetic farms, so what we test is exactly what the farmer's phone runs.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Advice for each field, not one calendar for the whole province.

- Water savings: on a test field, changing from rice-rice-rest to rice-squash-mungbean cuts irrigation from 535 to 257 mm per year and adds about 30 kg/ha of nitrogen.

- Fewer bags of urea when legumes are added to the rotation.

- Damage numbers the Department of Agriculture and the City Agriculture Office can use in reports.

- Harvest timing for planning dryers, mills and buyers.

VALIDATION

- 90.4% of the rice pixels we classify fall inside BSWM's official mapped key rice areas.

- Our gross return per hectare is within 2% of PSA's published figure.

- The soil-map reader placed 99.9% of cells correctly on a test sheet.

- Next step: ground-truth GPS points with the City Agriculture Office.

TOOLS

Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Leaflet, Python, Node.js, GitHub Actions.

CREATIVITY

- The farmer types nothing. Crop, soil, drainage and history are read from space.

- Each 20 m pixel's growth stage comes from its own planting date.

- One engine serves one field or the whole city.

- The analysis runs on the farmer's own phone, and farm boundaries are not uploaded or stored.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

- Low-end phones and weak signal.

- Plain words, with crop names in Filipino and Cebuano.

- Stating limits openly: "before costs" where costs are not published, and which crops get the full report.

SDGs

SDG 2 Zero Hunger, SDG 13 Climate Action, SDG 15 Life on Land, SDG 6 Clean Water and Sanitation, SDG 12 Responsible Consumption and Production.
